deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE PAGE IS. This is a table of quadratic residues, one prime per entry, with no derivations. The primes are 181, 191, 193, 197, 199, 211, 223, 227 and 229. It continues the previous page (131–179) and the next page (233–271).

THE MARKS ON THE PRIMES.
- A '+' written over the prime means p ≡ 1 (mod 4): 181, 193, 197, 229.
- A bar over the prime means p ≡ 3 (mod 4): 191, 199, 211, 223, 227.

WHAT EACH ENTRY LISTS.
- For p ≡ 1 (mod 4), -1 is a residue, so the residues are symmetric (a and p−a). Gauss lists only the residues in 1..(p−1)/2 and writes ± (or ∓) in front.
  - 181: 45 entries, the last being 87 (since (90/181) = −1).
  - 193: 48 entries, ending at 96.
  - 197: 49 entries, ending at 97.
  - 229: 57 entries, ending at 111.
- For p ≡ 3 (mod 4), all (p−1)/2 residues in 1..p−1 are listed after a '+'. For example, 191 has 95 entries ending at 184, and 211 ends at 209.

SPOT CHECKS (mine, by quadratic reciprocity):
- p = 181 (≡ 5 mod 8): 2 is absent, correct since (2/181) = −1. 3 and 5 are present (181 ≡ 1 mod 12 and mod 5). 7 is absent, since (7/181) = (6/7) = −1. 87 is present, since (3/181) = (29/181) = 1.
- p = 193 (≡ 1 mod 8): 2 is present. 5, 11 and 13 are absent. The inserted 65 is correct, since (5/193)(13/193) = (−1)(−1) = 1.
- p = 199: the interlinear insertions are all correct residues.
  - 33: (3/199)(11/199) = (−1)(−1).
  - 66: also uses (2/199) = 1.
  - 89: (89/199) = (21/89) = (2/3)(5/7) = 1.
- p = 223: the inserted 68 is correct, since (17/223) = (2/17) = 1. 67 is rightly absent. The struck entry between 94 and 98 is rightly deleted, since 95, 96 and 97 are all non-residues.
- p = 227:
  - Between 59 and 62 a struck entry is rightly deleted, since (60/227) = (61/227) = −1.
  - 131 and 132 are residues.
  - 133 is a residue: (7/227) = (19/227) = 1.
  - 134 is a residue: (2/227) = (67/227) = −1.
  - 135 is a non-residue: (5/227) = −1.
  - So the reading '132.133.134.136' is right, and the blot before 136 is a deleted wrong entry (probably 135).

THE VERTICAL STROKES (my identification). In the p ≡ 1 (mod 4) entries 181, 197 and 229, the strokes fall exactly at p/8, p/4 and 3p/8. They divide the half-range into octants, and Gauss is counting residues per octant.
- 181: the strokes come after 20, 45 and 67 (p/8 = 22.6, p/4 = 45.25, 3p/8 = 67.9). The counts per octant are 12, 13, 12, 8, which total 45.
- 197: strokes after 24, 49 and 70 (24.6, 49.25, 73.9). The counts are 12, 15, 12, 10.
- 229: strokes after 27, 57 and 85 (28.6, 57.25, 85.9). The counts are 16, 15, 14, 12.
- The same device appears on the previous page (139, 151, 163, with strokes at multiples of p/8 over the full range).

THE QUARTER-INTERVAL EXCESS (my addition). Residues minus non-residues in (0, p/4):
- 181: 25 − 20 = 5.
- 197: 27 − 22 = 5.
- 229: 31 − 26 = 5.

By the classical formula h(−4p) = 2·Σ_{a<p/4} (a/p) for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), this would give h(−724) = h(−788) = h(−916) = 10. That is my inference, not written on the page.

PURPOSE. These counts relate residue distribution to class numbers of binary quadratic forms, and the octant data to the quartic character of 2 and related biquadratic questions. Both were research interests of Gauss. The page itself only records the raw data.
errors: No errors found in the spot-checked entries; struck-out entries (199, 223, 227 rows) are self-corrections of wrong entries, and the interlinear insertions (65 at 193; 33, 66, 89 at 199; 68 at 223; 134 at 227) are correct residues.
Only sample checks were made by hand; the full lists should be verified by machine (see checkable).

results.what: Hand-computed table of all quadratic residues mod primes 181–229 (half-range for p≡1 mod 4, full range for p≡3 mod 4)
results.modern_name: Table of quadratic residues / Legendre symbol table
results.usually_credited_to: Such tables were made by Legendre and Gauss; DA (1801) contains residue tables

results.what: Partition of the residues by strokes at p/8, p/4, 3p/8, i.e. counting residues in octants of (0,p/2)
results.modern_name: Distribution of quadratic residues in intervals; Dirichlet-type class number formulas; octant counts related to the quartic character of 2
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet (1839–40) for the interval class-number formulas; Gauss's own unpublished work on class number and biquadratic residues is known (Werke II)

deep.surprise_reason: A routine residue table. The only non-trivial feature is the systematic octant/quarter marking, which shows Gauss collecting empirical data on residue counts in intervals. This is consistent with his known (partly unpublished) class-number and biquadratic investigations, so it is not new.
